title: Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
summary: A complete working grammar for SSC: parts of speech, tenses, subject-verb agreement, articles, prepositions, conjunctions, modals, conditionals, comparison, question tags, non-finites and inversion. It is rarely asked by name, but it decides roughly 7 Tier 1 questions (error spotting, sentence improvement, fill in the blanks, voice and narration) and about 10 in Tier 2.

subtopics.title: Parts of speech: nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs
subtopics.concept: Every word in a sentence does one of eight jobs. An error in grammar usually means a word is doing the wrong job. For example, a noun may stand where an adverb is needed. First find the job the slot needs. Then pick the word that does that job.

tricks.title: Cover the other name
tricks.body: When a pronoun sits next to a noun (*Ravi and I / Ravi and me*), cover the noun. Read the sentence with the pronoun alone. The form that sounds right is the answer.

example.q: The award was shared by Meena and ___. (I / me)
steps: Cover 'Meena and'.
'Shared by ___' needs an object form after the preposition 'by'.
Say it: 'shared by me'.

tricks.title: Scan every noun
tricks.body: In an error-spotting sentence, circle each noun. Ask two questions. Can I count it? Is it one of the special groups (no plural, always plural, cattle-type)? Words like informations, furnitures and advices are favourite errors.

example.q: He gave me some useful advices before the interview.
steps: 'Advice' has no plural.
Write 'some useful advice'.
To count it, say 'two pieces of advice'.

tricks.title: Few or a few: empty or half full
tricks.body: *Few* and *little* mean the glass is nearly empty (a negative feeling). *A few* and *a little* mean there is something (a positive feeling). Let the rest of the sentence show the feeling.

example.q: He had ___ friends in the new city, so he felt lonely. (few / a few)
steps: Feeling lonely is a negative result.
A negative feeling needs 'few' (hardly any).

tricks.title: Adjective order and word families
tricks.body: Adjectives follow the order OSASCOMP: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose. Example: a beautiful small old round brown Indian wooden table. Some adjectives have no degrees: unique, perfect, ideal, complete, entire, round, square, supreme, universal. So *more unique* is wrong. Learn word families: succeed, success, successful, successfully; courage, encourage, courageous; strength, strengthen, strong; beauty, beautify, beautiful; anger, angry, angrily.

tricks.title: Numbers with nouns
tricks.body: After a definite number, *dozen, hundred, thousand, million, score, lakh, crore* and *pair* take no -s: *three dozen eggs, five hundred rupees*. But *dozens of eggs* and *hundreds of people* keep the -s. A number + noun used as an adjective takes a hyphen and the noun stays singular: *a five-year plan, a ten-rupee note, a two-hour delay*.

tricks.title: Where adverbs go
tricks.body: Frequency words go before the main verb but after *be*: *He always comes late. He is always late.* Use *very* with the plain adjective and with -ing adjectives (very tall, very interesting). Use *much* with comparatives and many -ed words (much taller, much obliged).

mistakes.wrong: Making a no-plural noun plural: furnitures, informations, luggages, sceneries.
mistakes.right: Keep it singular: furniture, information, luggage, scenery.

mistakes.wrong: Using myself as a subject: Ravi and myself will attend.
mistakes.right: Use I: Ravi and I will attend.

mistakes.wrong: Writing elder than.
mistakes.right: With than, say older than: she is older than me.

mistakes.wrong: Using less with countable nouns: less mistakes.
mistakes.right: Use fewer with countable nouns: fewer mistakes.

mistakes.wrong: Adding a second negative to hardly or scarcely: I could not hardly breathe.
mistakes.right: Hardly is already negative: I could hardly breathe.

mistakes.wrong: Adding -s to dozen, hundred or lakh after a number: five hundreds rupees.
mistakes.right: Keep it plain after a number: five hundred rupees.

subtopics.notes:
### The eight jobs of a word
| Part of speech | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | names a person, place, thing or idea | **Honesty** pays. |
| Pronoun | replaces a noun | **She** called **us**. |
| Adjective | describes a noun or pronoun | a **brave** soldier |
| Verb | shows an action or a state | He **writes**. She **is** tired. |
| Adverb | describes a verb, adjective or adverb | runs **fast**, **very** tall |
| Preposition | links a noun to the rest of the sentence | sat **on** the wall |
| Conjunction | joins words or clauses | tea **or** coffee |
| Interjection | shows sudden feeling | **Alas!** He is gone. |

> **Rule:** Ask what the slot needs: noun, adjective, adverb or verb. Then choose the word of that type.

### Nouns that break the usual rules
| Group | Words | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| No plural (uncountable) | information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, scenery, poetry, jewellery, evidence, knowledge, traffic, bread | singular verb; count with *a piece of*: *two pieces of advice* |
| Always plural | scissors, trousers, spectacles, tongs, pliers, thanks, alms, premises, riches, outskirts, surroundings, belongings, proceeds | plural verb; *a pair of scissors* takes a singular verb |
| Singular form, plural meaning | cattle, police, people, poultry, clergy, gentry, vermin, peasantry | plural verb: *The police **are** here.* |
| Plural form, singular meaning | news, mathematics, physics, economics, civics, measles, mumps, billiards | singular verb: *The news **is** good.* |
| Same in singular and plural | sheep, deer, swine, series, species, aircraft | the verb or *a / two* shows the number |

### Collective nouns and the possessive
A collective noun names a group: team, committee, jury, family, audience, crowd, army.
- Group acts as one unit: singular verb. *The committee **has** approved the plan.*
- Members act separately: plural verb. *The jury **were** divided.*

The possessive shows ownership.
- Living things take *'s*: *the minister's car*. Non-living things take *of*: *the leg of the table*.
- Exceptions: time, distance, weight and personified things: *a day's leave, a stone's throw, the nation's pride*.
- One shop owned by both: *Ram and Shyam's shop*. Two shops: *Ram's and Shyam's shops*.

### Pronouns
| Situation | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| After a preposition (between, for, with, like) | object form | *between you and **me*** |
| After *than / as* | the form the hidden verb needs | *taller than **I** (am)*; *likes you more than **him*** |
| After *let* | object form | *Let **him and me** try.* |
| Complement of *be* (formal) | subject form | *It is **I**.* |
| Subject *one* | one's, oneself | *One must keep **one's** word.* |
| Order of persons | normal: 2nd, 3rd, 1st; admitting a fault: 1st, 2nd, 3rd | *You, he and I* / *I, you and he* |

- Words like *avail, absent, pride* need a -self pronoun: *He **availed himself of** the offer.*
- A -self pronoun is never a subject: *My friend and myself went* is wrong. Say *My friend and **I** went*.
- *Who* = subject (people). *Whom* = object (people). *Whose* = owner. *Which* = things.
- Use **that** after superlatives and after *all, only, same, none, nothing, everything*.
- *Either / neither* speak of two. *Any / none* speak of more than two. Traditional rule: *each other* (two), *one another* (more than two).
- A pronoun needs one clear owner and agrees with it: *Each of the girls brought **her** bag.*

### Adjectives
| Pair | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| few / a few / the few | hardly any / some / all of the small number | *The few books he had were old.* |
| little / a little / the little | same idea, uncountable | *There is **little** hope.* |
| many / much | countable / uncountable | *many chairs, much furniture* |
| fewer / less | countable / uncountable | ***fewer** people, **less** sugar* |
| elder / older | *elder* is for family, before a noun, never with *than* | *my **elder** sister*; *older than me* |
| latest / latter | time / order | *the **latest** news; the **latter** half* |
| farther / further | distance / extra | *two km **farther**; **further** details* |

### Adverbs and word forms
- **too** = more than needed: *too weak **to** walk*. **very** = a high degree. **enough** comes after the word: *old **enough***.
- *Hardly, scarcely, barely, seldom, rarely* are already negative: *I can **hardly** hear.*
- Look-alikes: *hard* (with effort) and *hardly* (almost not); *late* and *lately* (recently); *near* and *nearly* (almost); *high* and *highly* (very much).
Match the slot to the word type. A noun follows *the, his, of*. An adjective sits before a noun. An adverb follows an action verb.

After an action verb use an adverb: *She sings **beautifully**.* After a linking verb (be, seem, look, feel, smell, taste, sound, appear, become, grow) use an adjective: *The soup tastes **good**.*

> **Watch:** *Look* works both ways. *He looked **sad*** (seemed). *He looked **sadly** at the dog* (gazed).

patterns.name: Uncountable noun trap
patterns.howToSpot: A no-plural noun appears with -s (advices, furnitures, informations), or with many instead of much.
steps: Ask: can I count this noun one by one?
If not, drop the -s and use a singular verb.
Use much, little or some with it, not many.
Pick the option with the singular form.
patterns.why: The exam reuses the same short list of no-plural nouns every year.

example.q: She gave me many useful advices before the interview. Which part is wrong?
steps: 'Advice' cannot be counted.
It has no plural form.
Correct: 'some useful advice'.
example.answer: many useful advices -> some useful advice

patterns.name: Word-form family choice
patterns.howToSpot: A blank sits before a noun, after a preposition or after an action verb. The four options are forms of one word.
steps: Decide what the slot needs: noun, adjective, adverb or verb.
Find the signal: the, his or of before it means noun.
Before a noun means adjective. After an action verb means adverb.
Pick the option with that form.
patterns.why: Only one member of the family fits the job of the slot.

example.q: Hard work is the key to ___. (succeed / success / successful / successfully)
steps: 'Key to' is followed by a noun.
The noun of this family is 'success'.

patterns.name: Linking verb + adjective
patterns.howToSpot: The verb is be, seem, look, feel, smell, taste or sound, and one option is an -ly adverb.
steps: Test the verb: can 'is' or 'seems' replace it?
If yes, it is a linking verb.
A linking verb takes an adjective.
Reject the -ly adverb.
patterns.why: The adjective describes the subject, not the way the action is done.

example.q: The flowers smell ___. (sweet / sweetly)
steps: 'Smell' here means 'are sweet to the nose'.
That is a linking verb.
It takes the adjective 'sweet'.

patterns.name: Pronoun case and owner
patterns.howToSpot: A pronoun follows a preposition (between you and ___), acts as a subject, or must agree with its owner (its, their).
steps: Find the job of the pronoun: doer, receiver or owner.
Receiver or after a preposition: me, him, them.
Doer: I, he, they.
Owner: its, his, their, never it's.
patterns.why: The job of the pronoun fixes its form, not the way it sounds.

example.q: Between you and ___, the plan is weak. (me / I)
steps: 'Between' is a preposition.
After a preposition use the object form.

patterns.name: many / much and fewer / less
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits before a noun, and the options mix many, much, fewer, less.
steps: Can you count the noun? Chairs, people, errors: yes.
Countable: many or fewer.
Uncountable: much or less (furniture, sugar, time).
Match the option.
patterns.why: Each word is fixed to one kind of noun.

example.q: There is ___ sugar in the tea than in the coffee. (fewer / less)
steps: Sugar cannot be counted.
An uncountable noun takes 'less'.

patterns.name: Look-alike adverbs and hardly
patterns.howToSpot: The options are hard / hardly, late / lately, near / nearly, high / highly. Or a negative word sits next to hardly.
steps: Say the meaning: with effort, almost not, recently, almost, very much.
hard = with effort; hardly = almost not.
Hardly, scarcely and barely already mean 'almost not'.
Never add not or n't to them.
patterns.why: The -ly form is not always the adverb of the plain form; it often has a new meaning.

example.q: The old man could ___ walk without a stick. (hard / hardly)
steps: The meaning is 'almost not'.
'Hardly' means almost not.
'Hard' would mean 'with great effort'.

patterns.name: Verb after news, police, cattle
patterns.howToSpot: The subject is news, mathematics, police, people, cattle or scissors, and the options are is / are.
steps: Match the noun to its group.
news, mathematics, measles: singular verb.
police, people, cattle, scissors: plural verb.
Choose is or are to match.
patterns.why: The shape of the word (with -s or without) does not decide the number.

example.q: The news ___ good for the farmers. (is / are)
steps: 'News' looks plural but is singular.
A singular subject takes 'is'.

patterns.name: Possessive: 's or of
patterns.howToSpot: A noun shows ownership, and the options mix 's forms with of forms.
steps: Is the owner a living being? Use 's.
Is the owner a non-living thing? Use of.
Time, distance and weight take 's: a day's leave.
Two owners of one thing: 's on the last name only.
patterns.why: English marks ownership by 's for living things and by of for lifeless things.

example.q: Which is correct? (a) the table's leg (b) the leg of the table
steps: A table is not a living thing.
Non-living things take 'of'.

revision: Slot decides the word: noun after the, his, of; adjective before a noun; adverb after an action verb.
No plural: information, advice, furniture, luggage, news, machinery, scenery.
much + uncountable; many + countable plural; less + uncountable; fewer + countable.
Linking verbs (seem, look, feel, taste) take an adjective: tastes good.
Between you and me. Its has no apostrophe; it's means it is.
each other for two, one another for more than two (traditional exam rule).
Living things take 's; non-living things take of (leg of the table).

subtopics.title: Tenses and sequence of tenses
subtopics.concept: A tense shows when an action happens and whether it is finished, running or earlier than another action. You do not need to chant all twelve names. You need to know which **signal word** asks for which form. Underline the signal word first, then choose the verb form.

tricks.title: Scan for the signal word
tricks.body: Underline the time signal before reading the options. Since or for gives a perfect tense. Yesterday, ago or last gives the simple past. By + future time gives the future perfect. When, if or as soon as with future meaning gives the simple present.

example.q: She ___ in this bank for eight years now. (work)
steps: 'For eight years now' means the action began in the past.
It is still going on.
Use the present perfect continuous.

tricks.title: No will after when or if
tricks.body: If a clause starts with when, if, unless, until or as soon as and talks about the future, remove will from that clause. Will stays in the main clause only.

example.q: Unless you will apologise, she will not speak to you again. Which part is wrong?
steps: 'Unless' starts a condition clause.
A condition clause takes the simple present.
Correct: 'Unless you apologise'.

mistakes.wrong: Using the present perfect with a past time word: has gone yesterday.
mistakes.right: Use the simple past: went yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: Using will in an if or when clause: If it will rain.
mistakes.right: Use the present: If it rains, we will stay in.

mistakes.wrong: Writing since two years.
mistakes.right: Since needs a start point; for needs a length: for two years, since 2022.

mistakes.wrong: Using a state verb in the -ing form: I am understanding the problem.
mistakes.right: Use the simple form: I understand the problem.

mistakes.wrong: Changing a universal truth to the past in reported speech: said that the earth moved round the sun.
mistakes.right: Keep the present: said that the earth moves round the sun.

mistakes.wrong: Using the simple past for both of two past events.
mistakes.right: Give the earlier event had + V3: The train had left before we reached.

subtopics.notes:
### The 12 tenses at a glance
V1 is the base verb, V2 the past form, V3 the past participle (gone, taken).

| Tense | Form | Signal words | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple present | V1 / V1+s | always, usually, every day | The sun **rises** in the east. |
| Present continuous | is / am / are + V-ing | now, at present, look! | She **is writing** a report. |
| Present perfect | has / have + V3 | just, already, yet, ever, never, so far | I **have finished** my work. |
| Present perfect continuous | has / have been + V-ing | since, for, how long | He **has been waiting** for two hours. |
| Simple past | V2 | yesterday, ago, last year, in 2010 | We **met** him last week. |
| Past continuous | was / were + V-ing | when, while, at 8 pm yesterday | I **was reading** when you called. |
| Past perfect | had + V3 | before, after, already (in the past) | The train **had left** before we reached. |
| Past perfect continuous | had been + V-ing | for, since (in the past) | She **had been working** there for ten years. |
| Simple future | will / shall + V1 | tomorrow, next week, soon | I **will call** you tomorrow. |
| Future continuous | will be + V-ing | at this time tomorrow | We **will be travelling** at noon. |
| Future perfect | will have + V3 | by, by the time, by then | By March they **will have completed** it. |
| Future perfect continuous | will have been + V-ing | for ... by | By June he **will have been teaching** for 20 years. |

### Since and for
*Since* gives the start point (since Monday, since 2019). *For* gives the length (for three days). Both usually need a perfect tense.

- *I **have lived** here **since** 2019.* *I **have lived** here **for** six years.*
- *I live here since 2019* is wrong.
- Action still running: has / have been + V-ing. *It **has been raining** since morning.*
- A running action that ended before a past moment: had been + V-ing. *He was tired because he **had been walking** for six hours.*

> **Rule:** A definite past time word (yesterday, last week, in 2010) forbids the present perfect. *I **saw** him yesterday.* Not *I have seen him yesterday*.

### No future after time and if words
After *when, if, unless, until, till, before, after, as soon as, once, in case*, use the **present** tense. The meaning is still future.

- *I will call you when he **arrives**.* Not *will arrive*.
- *If it **rains**, the match will be cancelled.*
- *By the time* + present gives the future perfect: *By the time you **arrive**, I **will have left**.*
- *By the time* + past gives the past perfect: *By the time we **arrived**, the show **had begun**.*

> **Tip:** Strike out *will* in any clause that starts with when, if, unless or until. *Will* belongs only in the main clause.

### Two past actions
The earlier action takes **had + V3**. The later action takes the simple past.

- *The patient **had died** before the doctor **came**.*
- Hardly, scarcely or no sooner: past perfect first, simple past second. *No sooner **had** I **reached** the station **than** the train **left**.*
- *It is two years since* + simple past: *It is two years since he **left** the job.*
- *It is time / high time / about time* + subject + past form: *It is high time we **left**.*

### Sequence of tenses
A past main verb pulls the other clause into the past.

- *He said that he **was** busy.*
- Exception: universal truths and habits stay in the present. *The teacher said that water **boils** at 100 degrees Celsius.*

### Verbs that avoid the continuous
Some verbs describe states, not actions. They are not used in the -ing tenses: know, believe, understand, like, love, hate, want, prefer, own, possess, belong, contain, consist, seem, mean, see, hear, smell (when involuntary).

- *I **know** him.* Not *I am knowing him*.

Keep one time frame in a sentence unless the meaning changes. *She **opened** the door and **saw** a stranger.* Not *and sees a stranger*.

> **Watch:** Look for the signal word before you read the options. Then check the other clause for the same timeline.

patterns.name: Signal word fixes the tense
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has a time signal: yesterday, ago, last year, since, for, just, already, now, every day.
steps: Underline the signal word.
Read its tense from the table.
Pick the option with that form.
Reject look-alike forms from the next tense.
patterns.why: Each signal belongs to one tense family.

example.q: She ___ to Chennai last year. (moved / has moved / had moved / moves)
steps: 'Last year' is a finished past time.
A finished past time takes the simple past.

patterns.name: No future in the time or if clause
patterns.howToSpot: A future main clause (will ...) is joined to a clause starting with when, if, as soon as, until, unless or before.
steps: Spot the time or condition word.
Use the present tense in that clause, even for future meaning.
Keep will only in the main clause.
patterns.why: English uses the present form for a future event inside a time clause.

example.q: I will call you when I ___ home. (reach / will reach / reached / am reaching)
steps: 'When' starts a time clause.
A time clause takes the simple present.

patterns.name: Past perfect for the earlier past action
patterns.howToSpot: Two past actions are joined by before, after or when. The options mix had + V3 and V2.
steps: Put the two actions on a timeline.
Give the earlier one had + V3.
Give the later one the simple past.
Check the direction of before or after.
patterns.why: The past perfect exists to mark the earlier of two past events.

example.q: The patient had died before the doctor ___. (arrived / had arrived / arrives)
steps: The death happened first and already uses had + V3.
The doctor came later.
The later action takes the simple past.

patterns.name: Perfect continuous with since / for
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence measures how long an action lasted (since morning, for two years) and the action was running.
steps: Check that a duration is given and the action is running.
If it runs up to now: has / have been + V-ing.
If the frame is in the past: had been + V-ing.
Reject the simple and plain continuous forms.
patterns.why: Only the perfect continuous carries the idea 'from then until now'.

example.q: He was exhausted because he ___ for six hours. (walked / had been walking / has walked)
steps: The walking ran up to a past moment (the exhaustion).
That needs 'had been' + V-ing.

patterns.name: It is time / since + simple past
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has 'It is (high) time' or 'It is two years since'.
steps: Spot 'It is time' or 'since' after a length of time.
Use the simple past after it.
Reject the present or the future form.
patterns.why: These two frames are fixed: the verb after them is in the simple past.

example.q: It is high time we ___ for the station. (leave / left / will leave)
steps: 'It is high time' asks for the past form.
The subject is 'we'.

patterns.name: By the time
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence starts or joins with 'By the time'. The options mix will have + V3 and had + V3.
steps: Read the verb after 'by the time'.
Present verb there: main verb is will have + V3.
Past verb there: main verb is had + V3.
patterns.why: The tense after 'by the time' decides the tense of the main clause.

example.q: By the time we arrived, the show ___. (had begun / will have begun / has begun)
steps: 'Arrived' is past.
The show started earlier.
The earlier action takes had + V3.

patterns.name: State verbs stay simple
patterns.howToSpot: One option puts know, understand, like, want or own in the -ing form.
steps: Check if the verb is a state (know, believe, like, want, own).
State verbs are not used in -ing tenses.
Pick the simple form.
patterns.why: These verbs describe a state of mind or ownership, not an action in progress.

example.q: I ___ the answer to this question. (know / am knowing)
steps: 'Know' is a state verb.
State verbs do not take -ing.

revision: ago, last, yesterday: simple past. since, for, just, already: perfect family.
since + start point; for + length of time.
when, if, unless, until, as soon as + present tense, never will.
Earlier past action: had + V3. Later past action: simple past.
Still running: has / have been + V-ing. Ended before a past moment: had been + V-ing.
By the time + present: will have + V3. By the time + past: had + V3.
State verbs (know, like, want, own) do not take -ing.

subtopics.title: Subject-verb agreement (all rules and exceptions)
subtopics.concept: A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. That rule is easy. The trap is finding the **real subject**. Extra phrases often stand between the subject and its verb. Strike them out first.

tricks.title: Strike-through method
tricks.body: Draw a line through every phrase that starts with a preposition (of the boys, in the box, with his friends). Also strike every add-on phrase (as well as, along with, together with). What stays before the verb is the true subject.

example.q: The captain, together with his players, ___ felicitated. (was / were)
steps: Strike 'together with his players'.
Now read: 'The captain ___ felicitated'.
One captain, so singular: 'was'.

tricks.title: Nearest subject for or / nor pairs
tricks.body: For either ... or, neither ... nor, not only ... but also, or and nor, look only at the subject next to the verb. Put the plural subject second so the plural verb sounds natural.

example.q: Either the players or the coach ___ responsible. (is / are)
steps: Find the subject nearer the verb: 'the coach'.
It is singular.
Use 'is'.

tricks.title: The number and a number
tricks.body: *The number* is one figure, so it is singular. *A number* means many, so it is plural. Memory hook: A = Abundant.

mistakes.wrong: Matching the verb with the noun just before it: The list of items are ready.
mistakes.right: Match the head noun: The list of items is ready.

mistakes.wrong: Treating as well as or along with like and, and using a plural verb.
mistakes.right: The verb agrees with the first subject: The principal, as well as the teachers, was present.

mistakes.wrong: Using a plural verb after each, every, either or neither.
mistakes.right: Use a singular verb: Each of the girls was given a prize.

mistakes.wrong: Using a singular verb after one of those who.
mistakes.right: The who-clause describes the whole group: one of those people who never give up.

mistakes.wrong: Treating people, police and cattle as singular.
mistakes.right: They take a plural verb: The police are here.

mistakes.wrong: Using a plural verb for a sum of money or a distance treated as one amount.
mistakes.right: Use a singular verb: Fifty rupees is too much.

subtopics.notes:
### Find the real subject
Cover every phrase that starts with *of, in, with* and similar words. What is left is the subject.

> **Example:** *The quality **of the apples** **is** poor.* The subject is *quality*, so the verb is singular.

These add-on words never change the subject's number: **as well as, along with, together with, with, besides, in addition to, rather than, accompanied by, including, like, no less than**. The verb agrees with the first subject.

*The minister, along with his aides, **was** present.*

### Joined subjects
| Joined by | Verb agrees with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A **and** B | plural | Ravi and his sister **are** here. |
| A and B as one person or idea (one article) | singular | The secretary and treasurer **has** resigned. Bread and butter **is** my breakfast. |
| **each / every** before A and B | singular | Every boy and every girl **was** given a prize. |
| either ... or, neither ... nor, not only ... but also, or, nor | the **nearer** subject | Neither the teacher nor the students **were** late. |

### Always singular
- *Each, every, either, neither, everyone, someone, anyone, no one, nobody, everything* take a singular verb: *Each of the players **has** a kit.*
- *One of* + plural noun: singular. *One of my friends **is** a pilot.*
- *One of those* + plural noun + who: plural. *He is one of those people who **never give** up.*
- *The only one of ... who*: singular. *She is the only one of the girls who **has** passed.*
- *Many a* + singular noun: singular. *Many a man **has** tried.*
- *More than one* + singular noun: singular. *More than one student **was** absent.*
- An amount as one unit: singular. *Fifty rupees **is** too much. Ten km **is** a long way.*
- A gerund, an infinitive or a noun clause as subject: singular. *Walking **is** good exercise. What he said **was** false.*
- Titles and names, even with a plural form: *The United Nations **is** based in New York.*
- *A pair of, a series of, a set of* + plural noun: singular. *A pair of shoes **was** stolen.*

### Quantity words
- **A number of** = many, so plural. **The number of** = one figure, so singular. *A number of cars **were** towed. The number of cars **is** rising.*
- *Half, part, some, all, most, plenty, a lot, the rest, per cent, fractions* + **of X**: the verb agrees with X. *Half of the cake **is** eaten. Half of the guests **are** here.*
- *The* + adjective (a class of people): plural. *The rich **are** not always happy.*
- *There* or *here* + verb: the verb agrees with the noun that follows. *There **are** many reasons.*
- A relative pronoun takes the number of its owner word: *I, who **am** your friend, will help.*

### Collective nouns
Team, committee, jury, family, staff, audience, crowd, board and government are collective nouns.
- One body acting together: singular verb. *The team **is** strong.*
- Members acting separately: plural verb. *The team **are** arguing among themselves.*
- The matching pronoun follows the same choice (*its* or *their*).

### Quick lists
- **Singular:** news, mathematics, economics, measles, furniture, information, luggage, scenery.
- **Plural:** cattle, police, people, poultry, clergy, scissors, trousers, spectacles.
- **Depends on the noun after of:** all, some, most, half, a lot, plenty, the rest, two-thirds.

> **Tip:** In a divided-part item, the error is nearly always in the verb part. Strike the *of* or *as well as* phrase, then test the verb.

patterns.name: Head noun before an 'of' phrase
patterns.howToSpot: A phrase like the quality of, the list of, the bouquet of, or one of the sits before the verb.
steps: Find the head noun: quality, list, bouquet, one.
Ignore the phrase that starts with of.
Match the verb to the head noun.
patterns.why: The word 'of' begins a description, not a second subject.

example.q: The bouquet of roses ___ on the table. (is / are / were / have)
steps: The head noun is 'bouquet'.
It is singular.
Choose 'is'.

patterns.name: Each, every, one of: fixed singular
patterns.howToSpot: The subject begins with each, every, everyone, everybody, either, neither or 'one of the ...'.
steps: Check that the subject word is on the singular list.
Choose the singular verb even if a plural noun follows 'of'.
Reject the plural option that only sounds natural.
patterns.why: These words point to members one at a time, so the verb stays singular.

example.q: Each of the girls ___ given a certificate. (was / were / are / have)
steps: The subject word is 'each'.
'Each' is singular.

patterns.name: Nearer subject for neither ... nor
patterns.howToSpot: Two subjects are joined by neither ... nor, either ... or or not only ... but also, and they differ in number.
steps: Find the subject nearer the verb.
Match the verb to that subject alone.
Ignore the farther subject.
patterns.why: The nearer subject decides the verb, whatever the other subject is.

example.q: Neither the manager nor the workers ___ present. (were / was / is / has)
steps: The nearer subject is 'the workers'.
It is plural.
Choose 'were'.

patterns.name: Collective nouns and special singular subjects
patterns.howToSpot: The subject is a collective noun (committee, team), an -ics subject, 'more than one ...' or an amount (ten kilometres).
steps: Check the special singular list.
A group acting as one unit takes a singular verb.
Ignore the plural look of the nearest noun.
patterns.why: These subjects name one unit or one idea, whatever their shape.

example.q: More than one student ___ selected. (was / were / have / are)
steps: 'More than one' is followed by a singular noun.
The verb is singular.

patterns.name: A number of and the number of
patterns.howToSpot: The subject starts with 'a number of' or 'the number of' followed by a plural noun.
steps: Read the first word: a or the.
A number of means many, so use a plural verb.
The number of means one figure, so use a singular verb.
patterns.why: The word before 'number' shows whether you count many things or one figure.

example.q: The number of cars on the road ___ rising every year. (is / are)
steps: The phrase is 'the number of'.
It stands for one figure.
Use the singular 'is'.

patterns.name: Half, some, all + of X
patterns.howToSpot: The subject is half, some, all, most, a lot or a fraction followed by 'of' and a noun.
steps: Find the noun after 'of'.
Singular or uncountable noun: singular verb.
Plural noun: plural verb.
patterns.why: These words are only quantities; the noun after 'of' shows the number.

example.q: Half of the guests ___ already here. (is / are)
steps: The noun after 'of' is 'guests'.
It is plural.
Use 'are'.

patterns.name: The rich, and one of those who
patterns.howToSpot: The subject is 'the + adjective' (the rich, the poor) or the phrase 'one of those ... who'.
steps: 'The + adjective' names a class of people: plural verb.
In 'one of those + plural noun + who', the who-clause is about the group.
So use a plural verb after 'who'.
patterns.why: The verb agrees with the group, not with the word 'one'.

example.q: He is one of those students who ___ hard every day. (work / works)
steps: 'Who' stands for 'those students'.
That group is plural.
Use 'work'.

revision: Strike the of, with or as well as phrase; the head noun decides the verb.
each, every, everyone, either, neither: singular verb.
neither ... nor, either ... or: the verb follows the nearer subject.
A number of: plural. The number of: singular.
more than one, many a, amounts, mathematics, news, titles: singular.
half, some, all, most + of X: the verb agrees with X.
The error in a divided-part item usually sits in the verb part.

subtopics.title: Articles (a, an, the, zero article) and determiners
subtopics.concept: Articles are the small words a, an and the. Choose **a or an by the first sound** of the next word, not by its spelling. Use **the** for a particular or unique thing. Some nouns take no article at all. Small words like few, little, each and every are determiners and also decide marks.

tricks.title: Say it aloud
tricks.body: For a or an, whisper the next word. A vowel sound (on-est, em-el-ay, ex-ray) needs **an**. A y or w sound (you-niversity, won-day) needs **a**.

example.q: He is ___ one-eyed man and ___ honest worker. (a / an)
steps: 'One' sounds like 'won', a consonant sound: a one-eyed man.
'Honest' sounds like 'on-est': an honest worker.

tricks.title: The geography rule of thumb
tricks.body: Plural names, water and chains take **the**: the Alps, the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Andamans. A single peak, a single lake, a city or most countries take no article: Mount Abu, Lake Dal, Delhi, Nepal.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing a or an by spelling: an university, a hour, an European.
mistakes.right: Go by sound: a university, an hour, a European.

mistakes.wrong: Using the with meals, games and languages: play the cricket, the English is easy.
mistakes.right: Leave out the: play cricket, English is easy.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping the before superlatives or same and only.
mistakes.right: Use the: the best, the same, the only.

mistakes.wrong: Using the with a single mountain or lake: the Mount Everest.
mistakes.right: Use no article: Mount Everest.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving out a in rates and fixed phrases: twice week, in hurry.
mistakes.right: Write: twice a week, in a hurry.

subtopics.notes:
### A or an: go by the first sound
| Use **an** (vowel sound) | Use **a** (consonant sound) |
|---|---|
| an hour, an honest man, an heir, an honour | a university, a unit, a European, a useful tip |
| an MLA, an MBA, an SP, an X-ray, an LLB | a one-day match, a one-way street, a ewe, a union |
| an FIR, an NGO, an 8-year-old | a U-turn, a uniform, a hotel (the h is sounded) |

Letters whose names start with a vowel sound: A, E, F, H, I, L, M, N, O, R, S, X. So we say *an F-grade, an M.Sc., an S-bend*.

> **Tip:** Say the next word aloud. *University* begins with the sound "yu", so use **a**. *Hour* begins with a vowel sound, so use **an**.

### When to use a or an
- First mention of one countable thing: *I saw **a** cat.*
- A job or class: *She is **a** doctor.*
- A rate: *60 km **an** hour, twice **a** week, Rs 50 **a** kilo.*
- Fixed phrases: *what **a** sight, such **a** fool, quite **a** crowd, half **an** hour, **a** few, **a** little, **a** lot of, in **a** hurry, as **a** rule, at **a** loss.*

### When to use the
| Use | Example |
|---|---|
| Already mentioned or specific | *I bought a pen. **The** pen leaks.* |
| Unique things | *the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth* |
| Superlatives and ordinals | *the best, the first, the last, the only, the same* |
| Rivers, seas, oceans, canals, gulfs | *the Ganga, the Arabian Sea, the Suez Canal* |
| Mountain ranges, island groups, deserts | *the Himalayas, the Andamans, the Thar* |
| Holy books, epics, newspapers, famous buildings | *the Gita, the Ramayana, the Hindu, the Taj Mahal* |
| Countries with plural names or Republic, Union, States | *the USA, the UK, the Netherlands, the Maldives* |
| Musical instruments | *She plays **the** sitar.* |
| Adjective for a whole class | *the rich, the poor, the blind* |
| A whole species | ***The** tiger is a national animal.* |
| Double comparative | ***The** more you read, **the** better you write.* |
| A proper noun used as a common noun | *Kalidas is **the** Shakespeare of India.* |
| Directions | *in **the** north* (but *go north*) |

### When to use no article
- Names of people, cities, most countries, single mountains and single lakes: *Mount Everest, Lake Chilika, India*.
- Languages and school subjects: *He speaks Hindi. Physics is hard.*
- Meals, games and most diseases: *have lunch, play cricket, suffer from malaria*. But: *a heavy lunch, the flu, a cold*.
- General abstract and material nouns: *Honesty is the best policy. Gold is costly.* But: *the gold of Kolar*.
- *Man* meaning mankind: *Man is mortal.*
- School, church, hospital, prison, bed, college used for their main purpose: *go to school*. But: *went to the school to meet the principal*.
- Fixed phrases: *by bus, by train, at night, next week, last year, by chance, in time*.

### Determiners
| Word | Goes with | Note |
|---|---|---|
| each | singular, a group of two or more | *each side of the road* |
| every | singular, three or more as a whole | *every student* |
| some / any | some: positive and offers; any: negative and questions | *Would you like some tea?* |
| much / little / less | uncountable | *much time, less water* |
| many / few / fewer | countable plural | *many books, fewer errors* |

*Few / a few* and *little / a little*: *few* and *little* mean hardly any. *A few* and *a little* mean some. *He is new here and has **few** friends.*

patterns.name: A or an by first sound
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits before a word whose spelling and sound disagree: hour, honest, heir, university, European, one-, MLA, X-ray.
steps: Say the next word aloud.
Catch its first sound.
Vowel sound: an. Consonant sound: a.
Reject the option chosen by spelling.
patterns.why: The rule is about sound, and the exam words are a small fixed set.

example.q: She is ___ MLA from Bihar. (an / a / the / one)
steps: 'MLA' is said 'em-el-ay'.
It starts with a vowel sound.
Use 'an'.

patterns.name: Compulsory the
patterns.howToSpot: The blank comes before a unique thing, a superlative, a river or range, a direction or a second mention.
steps: Check the triggers: unique, superlative, second mention, geographical name, direction, adjective for a class.
If one fires, choose the.
If none fires, think of a, an or no article.
patterns.why: 'The' marks one specific thing, and each trigger names such a thing.

example.q: ___ Ganga is a holy river. (The / A / An / No article)
steps: 'Ganga' is a river.
River names take 'the'.

patterns.name: Zero article traps
patterns.howToSpot: An article sits before a language, a meal, a purpose-building, or 'man' meaning mankind.
steps: Ask: is the noun used for its purpose (go to school means to study)?
Languages, meals and mankind take no article.
In a divided sentence, the part with the wrong article is the error.
patterns.why: Nouns used for their purpose behave like general ideas, not like particular places.

example.q: The man is mortal. Improve the sentence.
steps: 'Man' here means the human race.
The human race takes no article.
Correct: 'Man is mortal'.

patterns.name: Few / a few, little / a little
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits before a countable plural (friends, days) or an uncountable noun (time, hope), and the options are few, a few, little, a little.
steps: Countable plural: few family. Uncountable: little family.
Read the feeling: positive means some, so a few or a little.
Negative means almost none, so few or little.
Match the option.
patterns.why: The small word 'a' turns 'hardly any' into 'some'.

example.q: Give me ___ time to think; I am almost done. (a little / little / the little / a few)
steps: 'Time' is uncountable.
'Almost done' is positive: you need some time.
Use 'a little'.

patterns.name: Article before a rate or a fixed phrase
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has a rate (per hour, per week) or a phrase like in a hurry, as a rule, what a sight.
steps: Spot the rate or the fixed phrase.
Rates and these phrases use a or an.
Check the sound of the next word for a or an.
patterns.why: These are fixed phrases with the article built in.

example.q: The car travels at 60 km ___ hour. (a / an / the / no article)
steps: A rate takes 'a' or 'an'.
'Hour' starts with a vowel sound.
Use 'an'.

patterns.name: Geographical names
patterns.howToSpot: The blank comes before a river, sea, mountain range, island group, desert, lake, single peak or city.
steps: Ask: is it plural, water or a chain?
If yes, use the.
If it is one peak, one lake, a city or most countries, use no article.
patterns.why: English marks groups, chains and water bodies with 'the' and single places without it.

example.q: We trekked in ___ Himalayas last summer. (the / a / no article)
steps: The Himalayas are a mountain range.
A range takes 'the'.

patterns.name: Each, every, some, any
patterns.howToSpot: The blank comes before a noun and the options are each, every, some, any.
steps: Each: one of two or more, seen one by one. Every: all of three or more.
Some: positive sentences and offers. Any: negatives and questions.
Match the option to the sentence type.
patterns.why: Determiners also have fixed jobs by sentence type.

example.q: Would you like ___ tea? (some / any)
steps: This is an offer.
Offers take 'some'.

revision: an hour, an MLA, an honest man; a university, a European, a one-rupee coin.
the: second mention, unique things, superlatives, rivers, ranges, directions, the + adjective.
no article: languages, meals, games, most diseases, man (mankind), general plurals.
go to school, church, hospital, bed: no article when used for their purpose.
few, little = hardly any; a few, a little = some.
each: two or more; every: three or more as a whole.

subtopics.title: Prepositions and conjunctions
subtopics.concept: A preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence. A conjunction joins words or clauses. Most questions test fixed pairs, like *fond of* or *no sooner ... than*. You cannot work these out by logic. Learn them as pairs and match the partner.

tricks.title: Find the partner
tricks.body: When you see hardly, scarcely, no sooner, not only, neither, either, both, whether, lest or though, look ahead for its fixed partner. A wrong or missing partner is very often the error.

example.q: Scarcely had the match started than it began to rain heavily. Which word is wrong?
steps: 'Scarcely' pairs with 'when' or 'before'.
'Than' belongs to 'no sooner'.

tricks.title: Group prepositions by meaning
tricks.body: Stopping: prevent, refrain, abstain, desist **from**. Dependence: depend, rely, count **on**. Skill: good, expert, adept **at**; proficient **in**. Latin comparatives: senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer **to**. One group takes one preposition.

mistakes.wrong: Adding a preposition after discuss, reach, enter, resemble, request or comprise.
mistakes.right: Use no preposition: discuss the plan, reach the station.

mistakes.wrong: Using between for more than two people or things.
mistakes.right: Use among for more than two: among the villagers.

mistakes.wrong: Writing prefer X than Y.
mistakes.right: Write prefer X to Y.

mistakes.wrong: Using though ... but, because ... so or both ... as well as.
mistakes.right: Use one conjunction, or the true pair: both ... and.

mistakes.wrong: Adding not after unless, lest or until.
mistakes.right: These words already carry a negative: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

mistakes.wrong: Using since with a length of time: since three days.
mistakes.right: Use for with a length: for three days.

subtopics.notes:
### Time and place
| Word | Time | Place |
|---|---|---|
| **at** | exact point: at 6 pm, at noon, at night | point or address: at the gate |
| **on** | days and dates: on Monday, on 15 August | surface or street: on the table |
| **in** | months, years, seasons, parts of day: in May, in 2025 | enclosed area, city, country: in Delhi |
| **by** | not later than: by 5 pm | beside or means: by the window, by train |
| **till / until** | up to a time: wait till 5 | |
| **since / for** | start point / length, with perfect tenses | |
| **between / among** | two / more than two | between the banks, among the villagers |
| **beside / besides** | next to / in addition to | sat beside me; besides English he knows Tamil |
| **into / in** | movement inside / position | jumped into the pool; swimming in the pool |

### Fixed prepositions
| Pair | Sense |
|---|---|
| abide by, comply with | follow a rule |
| accede to, insist on, depend on, rely on | agree; demand; trust |
| accuse of, guilty of, charge with | blame for a crime |
| afraid of, capable of, fond of, proud of, sure of, aware of | fear; able; like; pride; certain; knowing |
| angry with (person), angry at (thing) | anger |
| agree with (person), to (proposal), on (point) | agreement |
| apologise to (person) for (act) | say sorry |
| good at, weak in, succeed in, interested in | skill; achieve; keen |
| married to, similar to, indifferent to, addicted to, acquainted with | link |
| prevent, refrain, abstain from | stop |
| die of (disease), die from (cause) | death |
| differ from (thing), differ with (view) | disagree |
| divide into (parts), divide among (people) | share |
| senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior to; prefer X to Y | comparison |
| tired of (bored), tired from (exhausted) | fatigue |
| wait for (someone), wait on (serve) | waiting |
| deal in (goods), deal with (handle) | trade; handle |
| part with (thing), part from (person) | give up; leave |
| object to + V-ing, congratulate on, deprive of, eligible for | fixed |

**No preposition after these verbs:** discuss (the plan), describe, reach (the station), enter (the room), marry (someone), attack, resemble, request, order, answer (a question), comprise, emphasise, investigate.

> **Watch:** *Discuss about, reach at* and *comprises of* are wrong. Say *consists of* or *is composed of*.

### Joining pairs
| Pair | Example |
|---|---|
| either ... or / neither ... nor | *Neither he nor I knew.* |
| both ... and | *both Ravi **and** Sita* (not *as well as*) |
| not only ... but also | *She **not only** sings **but also** dances.* |
| whether ... or | *whether you like it **or** not* |
| no sooner ... than | *No sooner had he left **than** it rained.* |
| hardly / scarcely / barely ... when, before | *Hardly had I sat **when** the phone rang.* |
| though / although ... yet (or nothing) | *Though he is poor, he is honest.* Never *though ... but*. |
| so ... that / such ... that | *so tired **that** he slept* |
| such ... as / the same ... as | *such books **as** these* |
| lest ... should | *Walk carefully **lest** you **should** fall.* |
| rather ... than | *I would rather walk **than** wait.* |
| as ... as / not so ... as | *not so tall **as** his brother* |

### Errors to watch
- Two conjunctions for one job: *Although ... but, Because ... so, Since ... therefore* are wrong. Use one.
- *Unless, until, lest* and *till* already carry a negative: *Unless you do not work* is wrong.
- Say *The reason ... is that*, not *because*.
- Do not mix pairs: *Scarcely ... than* and *No sooner ... when* are wrong.
- Keep the joined parts alike: *He plays **not only** cricket **but also** football.* Not *He not only plays cricket but also football*.

patterns.name: at / on / in for time and place
patterns.howToSpot: The blank comes before a clock time, a day, a month, a city or a surface.
steps: Classify the word: exact point, day or date, month or large area, surface.
at: point. on: day or surface. in: month or enclosed area.
Choose the matching option.
patterns.why: The three words split time and space by how exact they are.

example.q: We reached the airport ___ 6 o'clock. (at / on / in / by)
steps: '6 o'clock' is an exact time.
An exact time takes 'at'.

patterns.name: Fixed preposition after a word
patterns.howToSpot: An adjective, noun or verb (fond, good, angry, insist, married) is followed by the blank.
steps: Find the governing word.
Recall its fixed pair.
Reject the prepositions that fit the meaning but not this word.
patterns.why: These pairs are conventions, and the exam reuses the same ones.

example.q: Ravi is very good ___ mathematics. (at / in / on / for)
steps: 'Good' is followed by 'at' when it means skill.
Choose 'at'.

patterns.name: Between / among and since / for
patterns.howToSpot: Two or more parties share something, or a time span starts or lasts.
steps: Count the sharers: two means between, more than two means among.
A start point means since. A length means for.
Choose the option that fits.
patterns.why: Each pair splits one idea by number or by the shape of the span.

example.q: The prize was divided ___ the two winners. (between / among / in / into)
steps: There are two winners.
Two parties take 'between'.

patterns.name: Joining pairs
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence opens with no sooner, hardly, scarcely or not only, and the blank is the second half of the pair.
steps: Recall the fixed partner: no sooner ... than; hardly, scarcely ... when; not only ... but also.
Eliminate mixed partners.
Choose the partner word.
patterns.why: These pairs are welded together; the first half fixes the second.

example.q: No sooner did the bell ring ___ the students rushed out. (than / when / then / that)
steps: 'No sooner' needs 'than'.
Choose 'than'.

patterns.name: No preposition after the verb
patterns.howToSpot: The verb is discuss, reach, enter, resemble, describe, marry or comprise, and one option adds a preposition.
steps: Spot the verb.
Check the no-preposition list.
Reject the option with 'about', 'at' or 'of'.
patterns.why: These verbs already carry the meaning of the preposition.

example.q: The committee will discuss ___ the new rules tomorrow. (about / on / no word)
steps: 'Discuss' takes its object directly.
Add no word.

patterns.name: Latin comparatives with to
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence compares two things with senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior or prefer, and one option uses than.
steps: Spot the Latin comparative.
It takes 'to', never 'than'.
Choose the option with 'to'.
patterns.why: Words like senior and prefer come from Latin comparatives that already contain the idea of 'than'.

example.q: She is senior ___ me in the office. (than / to / from / over)
steps: 'Senior' is a Latin comparative.
It takes 'to'.

patterns.name: Two conjunctions for one job
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has although or because and a second linking word such as but or so.
steps: Spot the first conjunction (although, because, since).
Look for a second one in the other clause.
Delete the second one.
patterns.why: One link needs one conjunction.

example.q: Although he was tired, but he finished the work. Which word is wrong?
steps: 'Although' already joins the two parts.
'But' repeats the job.

revision: at 6, on Monday, in May; at the door, on the table, in Bengaluru.
since + start point; for + length of time.
fond of, good at, angry at a thing, angry with a person, senior to, prefer to.
between = two, among = more than two.
No sooner ... than; hardly / scarcely ... when; not only ... but also.
No preposition after discuss, reach, enter, resemble, comprise.
Unless, lest, until already carry a negative.

subtopics.title: Modals, conditionals and the subjunctive
subtopics.concept: Modal verbs like can, may, must and should add a shade of meaning to the main verb. A conditional sentence joins an *if* clause to a result clause. The exam tests two things: the **form** after a modal, and the **matching of tenses** in a conditional.

tricks.title: Match the type by the if-clause
tricks.body: Read only the if-clause. Present simple: use will or can in the result. Past simple: use would in the result. Past perfect: use would have + V3.

example.q: If he had left earlier, he ___ the train. (would catch / would have caught / will catch)
steps: The if-clause is past perfect.
That is a third conditional.
The result needs 'would have + V3': 'would have caught'.

tricks.title: Modal + base form
tricks.body: After any modal the next verb is bare. If you see a modal followed by to, -s, -ing or -ed, that is the error. The only exceptions are ought to and used to.

mistakes.wrong: She can sings well.
mistakes.right: She can sing well. A modal takes the base form.

mistakes.wrong: You must to go now.
mistakes.right: You must go now.

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay home.
mistakes.right: If it rains, we will stay home.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have money, I would buy a car.
mistakes.right: If I had money, I would buy a car.

mistakes.wrong: If I was you, I would apologise.
mistakes.right: If I were you, I would apologise.

mistakes.wrong: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
mistakes.right: Unless you work hard, you will fail.

mistakes.wrong: You needn't to come.
mistakes.right: You needn't come.

subtopics.notes:
### What modals do
The modals are *can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to, need, dare, used to*. Three facts hold for all of them.
- A modal is followed by the **base form** of the verb: *She can swim.* Never *She can swims* or *can to swim*.
- A modal takes no -s in the third person: *He must go.*
- To make a question, put the modal first: *Can you help?*

> **Watch:** *Ought to* and *used to* keep **to**. *You ought to go.* But after *must, can, may, should* there is no *to*.

### Meanings
| Modal | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| can / could | ability; could is past ability or polite request | *He can drive. Could you help me?* |
| may / might | permission; possibility (might is weaker) | *May I come in? It might rain.* |
| must | strong duty; strong logical certainty | *You must wear a helmet.* |
| have to | outside rule; needs tense forms | *I had to leave early.* |
| should / ought to | advice, moral duty | *You should sleep early.* |
| need | necessity; in questions and negatives it can act as a modal | *You need not come. Need I come?* |
| dare | courage; modal in negatives and questions | *He dare not speak.* |
| will / shall | future; shall with I and we for offers | *Shall I open the window?* |
| would | past habit, polite request | *He would visit every summer.* |
| used to | past habit or state, now stopped | *I used to smoke.* |

### Modals with the perfect
- **should have / ought to have + V3:** a duty not done. *You should have called.*
- **could have + V3:** a chance that was missed. *She could have won.*
- **must have + V3:** a certain guess about the past. *He must have missed the train.*
- **may / might have + V3:** a possible guess about the past. *They might have left.*
- **needn't have + V3:** did it, but it was not needed. *You needn't have come.*
- **would have + V3:** the result clause of a past unreal condition.

### Conditionals
| Type | If-clause | Result clause | Sense |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zero | present simple | present simple | general truth: *If you heat ice, it melts.* |
| First | present simple | will / can / may + base | real future: *If it rains, we will stay.* |
| Second | past simple (were for all subjects) | would / could / might + base | unreal present: *If I were rich, I would travel.* |
| Third | past perfect | would have + V3 | unreal past: *If she had studied, she would have passed.* |

- Use **were** for all persons in a second-conditional if-clause: *If I were you.*
- Do not use *will* or *would* in the if-clause itself. *If it rains* is right; *If it will rain* is wrong.
- **Unless** = if not, and it already carries the negative: *Unless you hurry, you will miss it.*
- Inverted forms drop *if*: *Had I known, I would have come. Were he here, he would help. Should you need help, call me.*
- **Wish** takes the past for the present and the past perfect for the past: *I wish I knew. I wish I had gone.*
- **As if / as though** with an unreal situation takes the past: *He talks as if he owned the place.*

> **Tip:** In a third conditional both halves look back. If either half looks forward or present, the tense is wrong.

patterns.name: Modal + base form
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has can, may, must, should or will, and the next verb has -s, -ing, -ed or a to.
steps: Find the modal.
Look at the verb right after it.
If it is not the bare verb, that is the error.
patterns.why: Modals are helper verbs and carry the tense, so the main verb stays bare.

example.q: She can ___ five languages. (speaks / speak / speaking / to speak)
steps: The modal is 'can'.
The verb after it must be bare: 'speak'.

patterns.name: Shades of meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits in a sentence expressing duty, advice, permission, ability or a guess.
steps: Name the meaning: strong duty, advice, permission, ability, guess.
Match it: must, should, may, can, might.
Choose the modal for that meaning.
patterns.why: Each modal has one main job, and the stem tells you which job is needed.

example.q: You ___ wear a seat belt; it is the law. (must / might / could / would)
steps: The law is a strong duty.
Strong duty takes 'must'.

patterns.name: Modal + have + V3
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence talks about the past and the options include should have, must have, could have, needn't have.
steps: Find the clue: regret, certainty, missed chance or unneeded act.
Match: should have (duty), must have (certain guess), could have (chance), needn't have (not needed).
Choose the matching option.
patterns.why: The perfect form after a modal points back to a past event.

example.q: The road is wet, so it ___ rained last night. (must have / should have / would have)
steps: The wet road is a clue for a certain guess.
A certain guess about the past takes 'must have'.

patterns.name: Conditional tense matching
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has an if-clause and a blank in the result clause, or the reverse.
steps: Read the if-clause tense.
Present simple: will + base. Past simple: would + base. Past perfect: would have + V3.
Choose the option that matches.
patterns.why: Each conditional type pairs one if-tense with one result form.

example.q: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer. (am / was / were / be)
steps: The result has 'would', so this is a second conditional.
The if-clause takes 'were' for all persons.

patterns.name: Unless and inverted conditionals
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has unless, or starts with Had, Were or Should in place of if.
steps: Unless means if not, so keep the verb positive.
Had + subject + V3 means if + past perfect.
Should + subject + base means if + present.
patterns.why: Dropping if and inverting the subject gives the same meaning.

example.q: Unless you ___ hard, you will not pass. (study / do not study / will study / studied not)
steps: 'Unless' already means 'if not'.
The verb must stay positive: 'study'.

patterns.name: Wish and as if
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has wish, as if or as though, and the situation is unreal.
steps: Present unreal wish: use the past (I wish I knew).
Past unreal wish: use the past perfect (I wish I had gone).
Use were for all persons in the unreal present.
patterns.why: The unreal situation moves one step back in time.

example.q: I wish I ___ the answer now. (know / knew / had known / will know)
steps: The wish is about the present.
The verb goes back one step: past 'knew'.

patterns.name: Need, dare and used to
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has need, dare or used to in a negative, a question or a habit.
steps: Need and dare act as modals in negatives and questions, with no -s and no to.
Used to is a past habit that has stopped.
Check that the verb after it is bare.
patterns.why: These three verbs switch between modal and ordinary use.

example.q: You ___ come tomorrow; the meeting is cancelled. (needn't / don't need / needs not / need not to)
steps: 'Needn't' works as a modal.
It is followed by a bare verb, so 'needn't come' is right.

revision: Modal + bare verb; no -s; no to (except ought to and used to).
must = duty or certainty; should = advice; may = permission or possibility.
should have + V3 = duty not done; must have + V3 = certain guess about the past.
First: if + present, will + base. Second: if + past, would + base. Third: if + past perfect, would have + V3.
Use were for all subjects in the second conditional.
No will or would inside the if-clause.
Unless = if not; do not add a second negative.

subtopics.title: Degrees of comparison and question tags
subtopics.concept: Adjectives and adverbs have three degrees: positive, comparative and superlative. A question tag is the short question added to a statement, like *isn't it?*. Both follow strict patterns, so learn the pattern and check it.

tricks.title: Flip the polarity
tricks.body: Read the statement. Note whether it is positive or negative. Then use the helper verb with the opposite sign and a pronoun. Command? Use will you. Let's? Use shall we.

example.q: She has never lied to you, ___? (has she / hasn't she / does she / didn't she)
steps: 'Never' makes the statement negative.
The tag must be positive.
The helper is 'has': 'has she'.

tricks.title: Watch than, that of and other
tricks.body: When a comparison feels odd, check two things. First: are two like things compared (use *that of* or *those of*)? Second: does the comparison come from the same group (add *other*)?

mistakes.wrong: She is more cleverer than her sister.
mistakes.right: She is cleverer than her sister.

mistakes.wrong: This is the most best book.
mistakes.right: This is the best book.

mistakes.wrong: He is taller than any boy in the class.
mistakes.right: He is taller than any other boy in the class.

mistakes.wrong: The climate of Goa is better than Delhi.
mistakes.right: The climate of Goa is better than that of Delhi.

mistakes.wrong: He is senior than me.
mistakes.right: He is senior to me.

mistakes.wrong: Nobody came, didn't they?
mistakes.right: Nobody came, did they?

mistakes.wrong: I am late, amn't I?
mistakes.right: I am late, aren't I?

subtopics.notes:
### The three degrees
| Degree | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | equal or plain | *as tall as, so tall as* |
| Comparative | two things | *taller than, more careful than* |
| Superlative | three or more | *the tallest, the most careful* |

- Short words add -er and -est: *tall, taller, tallest*.
- Long words (three or more syllables) use *more* and *most*.
- Two-syllable words: -y words add -er (*happier*); most others use *more*.
- Never use both: *more better, most cleverest* are wrong.
- Irregular forms: **good/well - better - best; bad/ill - worse - worst; far - farther/further - farthest/furthest; little - less - least; much/many - more - most; old - older/elder - oldest/eldest**.

### Rules for comparatives
- The comparative takes **than**, not *then* or *from*. *She is taller than I am.*
- Compare like with like: *The climate of Shimla is cooler than **that** of Delhi.* Not *than Delhi*.
- Add *other* or *else* when a thing is compared with its own group: *Ravi is taller than any **other** boy in the class.*
- Do not add *other* to a superlative: *He is the best of all boys.*
- Latin comparatives take **to**: *senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable to*.
- **Elder / eldest** are used for family members only. *Older* works for anyone.
- **Later / latest** speak of time. **Latter / last** speak of order.
- **Farther** is distance. **Further** is more or additional: *further details*.
- **Double comparative:** *The more you practise, the better you get.*
- **Superlative sense in other forms:** *No other city is as big as Mumbai. Mumbai is bigger than any other city.*

### Question tags
A tag repeats the helper verb of the statement with the opposite polarity.
- **Positive statement, negative tag:** *She sings well, doesn't she?*
- **Negative statement, positive tag:** *He is not late, is he?*
- The tag uses a pronoun, not a noun: *Ravi is here, isn't **he**?*
- The tag verb copies the helper: *is, are, was, has, will, can*. If there is no helper, use **do, does, did**.

### Special cases
| Statement | Tag |
|---|---|
| I am | aren't I? |
| Let's | shall we? |
| Let us (asking permission) | will you? |
| Imperative (command) | will you? |
| Do (request) | won't you? |
| There is / are | isn't there? / aren't there? |
| Nobody, none, no one, neither, nothing | positive tag with **they** (it for nothing): *Nobody called, did they?* |
| Everybody, someone, anyone | they: *Everyone came, didn't they?* |
| Hardly, seldom, never, rarely, barely, few, little | positive tag: *He seldom lies, does he?* |
| Must (necessity) | needn't: *You must go, needn't you?* |
| Used to | didn't (or usedn't) |
| Had better | hadn't |
| Ought to | shouldn't |
| Would rather | wouldn't |
| I have (main verb, possession) | haven't or don't |

> **Tip:** A word with a negative meaning such as *hardly* or *seldom* makes the statement negative. So the tag is positive.

### Comparison of like parts
The two sides of *than* or *as* must be the same kind: a person with a person, a noun with a noun.
- Wrong: *Her handwriting is better than Sita.* Right: *than **that of** Sita* or *than **Sita's***.

patterns.name: Double comparative or superlative
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has more or most beside an -er or -est word, or beside an irregular comparative.
steps: Spot more or most.
Check the next word.
If it already has -er or -est, or is irregular, delete more or most.
patterns.why: One degree marker is enough.

example.q: She is more cleverer than her brother. Which words are wrong?
steps: 'Cleverer' is already a comparative.
'More' repeats it.

patterns.name: Than, to, and like with like
patterns.howToSpot: A comparison uses than, to, or compares something with a place or a person's belongings.
steps: Latin comparative (senior, junior, superior, prefer): use to.
Other comparatives: use than.
Check that both sides of than are alike; use that of or those of.
patterns.why: Two things compared must be the same type.

example.q: The population of India is larger than ___ of the USA. (that / those / it / the)
steps: Population is compared with population.
'Population' is singular, so use 'that'.

patterns.name: Any other and superlative sense
patterns.howToSpot: A comparative sentence has 'any', or a superlative sentence has 'other'.
steps: Is the thing part of the group it is compared with?
If yes, use 'any other' with the comparative.
Do not put 'other' in a superlative.
patterns.why: A thing cannot be compared with itself.

example.q: Mount Everest is higher than ___ mountain in the world. (any other / any / other)
steps: Everest is itself a mountain.
So the comparison needs 'any other'.

patterns.name: Question tag polarity
patterns.howToSpot: A statement ends in a comma and a short blank like ___?
steps: Is the statement positive or negative?
Use the opposite in the tag.
Copy the helper verb, or do/does/did, plus a pronoun.
patterns.why: The tag asks the listener to confirm the statement.

example.q: You have finished the work, ___? (haven't you / have you / don't you / do you)
steps: The statement is positive.
The tag is negative with helper 'have': 'haven't you'.

patterns.name: Special tag cases
patterns.howToSpot: The statement is a command, Let's, I am, there is, nobody or hardly/never/seldom.
steps: Command: will you. Let's: shall we. I am: aren't I.
There: isn't there.
Nobody, no one, hardly, seldom: positive tag.
patterns.why: These forms have fixed tags that do not follow the plain pattern.

example.q: Let's go for a walk, ___? (shall we / will we / don't we / won't we)
steps: The statement begins with 'Let's'.
'Let's' takes 'shall we'.

patterns.name: Elder / older, later / latter, farther / further
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits between two similar-looking comparatives.
steps: Family members: elder. Anyone: older.
Time: later. Order: latter.
Distance: farther. Extra or more: further.
patterns.why: Each pair has a narrow, fixed use.

example.q: My ___ brother is an engineer. (elder / older / oldest)
steps: 'Brother' is a family member.
'Elder' is used for family members.

patterns.name: Positive, comparative, superlative conversion
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence is to be changed from one degree to another with the same meaning.
steps: Superlative: no other X is as ... as Y.
Comparative: Y is ... than any other X.
Positive: not so ... as.
patterns.why: The same fact can be said in all three degrees.

example.q: Change to comparative: Delhi is the biggest city in north India.
steps: The superlative means the city is bigger than all others.
Use 'any other' with the comparative.
example.answer: Delhi is bigger than any other city in north India.

revision: Never use more or most with an -er or -est word.
Comparative takes than; Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) take to.
Add other when comparing with the rest of the same group.
Compare like with like: that of, those of.
Question tag: opposite polarity, helper verb, pronoun.
I am - aren't I; Let's - shall we; command - will you; there is - isn't there.
Nobody, hardly, seldom, never: statement is negative, tag is positive.

subtopics.title: Non-finites (infinitive, gerund, participle), inversion and parallelism
subtopics.concept: Non-finite verb forms are the infinitive (to go), the gerund (going) and the participle (going, gone). They do not show tense or number by themselves. Inversion means putting the helper verb before the subject, as in questions and after some negative words.

tricks.title: Preposition then -ing
tricks.body: If the word before the blank is a preposition (of, in, at, without, after, before, by, about), the verb must end in -ing. Watch for to in look forward to and used to: it is a preposition there.

example.q: She is looking forward to ___ you soon. (see / seeing / saw / seen)
steps: 'Look forward to' has 'to' as a preposition.
A preposition takes a gerund: 'seeing'.

tricks.title: Negative start means flip
tricks.body: When a sentence opens with never, rarely, hardly, no sooner, not only or not until, flip the first helper before the subject. If there is no helper, add do, does or did.

mistakes.wrong: She enjoys to dance.
mistakes.right: She enjoys dancing.

mistakes.wrong: He is interested to learn music.
mistakes.right: He is interested in learning music.

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to meet you.
mistakes.right: I look forward to meeting you.

mistakes.wrong: Hardly he had left when it rained.
mistakes.right: Hardly had he left when it rained.

mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a crowd.
mistakes.right: Never have I seen such a crowd.

mistakes.wrong: Walking down the road, the rain began.
mistakes.right: Walking down the road, I felt the rain begin.

mistakes.wrong: She asked where did he go.
mistakes.right: She asked where he went.

subtopics.notes:
### Infinitive and gerund
Some verbs are followed by an infinitive, some by a gerund, and a few by either.
| Follows | Verbs |
|---|---|
| **to + verb** | want, hope, decide, plan, promise, refuse, manage, afford, offer, learn, fail, agree, wish |
| **-ing** | enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, practise, suggest, deny, admit, consider, postpone, imagine, keep, escape |
| **either** (meaning same) | begin, start, like, love, hate, continue, prefer |
| **either** (meaning changes) | stop, remember, forget, try, regret |

- *He stopped **to smoke*** = he paused in order to smoke. *He stopped **smoking*** = he quit.
- *I remember **meeting** him* = I recall it. *Remember **to post** it* = do not forget the task.
- After a **preposition**, use the gerund: *She is fond **of singing**.* *He left **without saying** goodbye.*
- **To** as a preposition needs a gerund: *look forward to meeting, used to waking early, object to paying, be accustomed to working*.
### Bare infinitive and fixed patterns
- After **let, make, see, hear, help** the bare infinitive follows: *She made me **laugh**.* But in the passive the *to* returns: *I was made **to** laugh.*
- After **modal verbs, had better, would rather** use the bare verb.
- *It is worth, no use, no good, cannot help, be busy* + gerund: *It is no use **crying**.*
- The **split infinitive** puts a word between *to* and the verb (*to quickly run*). Exams prefer the unsplit form.

### Participles and their subjects
- **Present participle (-ing)** shows an action at the same time: *Walking home, I met him.*
- **Past participle (V3)** has a passive or completed sense: *Tired of waiting, she left.*
- A participle phrase at the start must belong to the subject that follows. Otherwise it dangles.
  - Wrong: *Walking down the street, the rain started.* Right: *Walking down the street, **I** felt the rain.*
- Perfect participle **having + V3**: *Having finished the work, he left.*

> **Watch:** After a participle phrase, ask "who did that action?" The subject of the main clause must answer.

### Inversion
Inversion puts the helper before the subject: *Rarely **have I seen** such a view.*
- **Questions:** *Where **did he go**?* The helper is before the subject.
- **Negative openers** force inversion: **never, rarely, seldom, hardly, scarcely, barely, no sooner, nowhere, little, not only, not until, under no circumstances, on no account, at no time**.
  - *Never **have I seen** such a crowd.*
  - *No sooner **had he left** than it rained.*
  - *Not only **did she sing**, but she also danced.*
  - *Hardly **had I sat** when the phone rang.*
- **So / neither / nor** agreement: *He likes tea, and **so do I**. She cannot swim, and **neither can he**.*
- **Conditional inversion:** *Had I known, ... Were he here, ... Should you need, ...*
- **Only + adverb** at the start: *Only then **did I realise** my mistake. Only after dinner **did she speak**.*
- Do **not** invert an embedded question: *I asked where he went.* Not *where did he go*.

> **Tip:** A sentence starting with a negative word and followed by the subject and then the verb is nearly always wrong.

patterns.name: Verb + infinitive or gerund
patterns.howToSpot: The blank follows a verb such as enjoy, avoid, hope, decide, mind or suggest.
steps: Find the main verb.
Check the verb list: gerund group or infinitive group.
Choose -ing or to + verb accordingly.
patterns.why: Each verb selects its own pattern, and the exam uses a fixed core set.

example.q: She avoided ___ to him. (to talk / talking / talk / talked)
steps: 'Avoid' takes a gerund.
Choose 'talking'.

patterns.name: Preposition + gerund
patterns.howToSpot: The blank comes right after a preposition, including 'to' in look forward to and used to.
steps: Identify the preposition.
Remember that a preposition is followed by a noun or gerund.
Change to -ing form.
patterns.why: A preposition needs a noun-like word after it.

example.q: He left without ___ goodbye. (say / to say / saying / said)
steps: 'Without' is a preposition.
The verb must be a gerund: 'saying'.

patterns.name: Dangling participles
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence begins with an -ing or -ed phrase followed by a comma and a subject.
steps: Ask who did the action in the phrase.
Does the subject after the comma answer that?
If not, change the subject or rewrite the phrase.
patterns.why: The opening phrase describes the noun right after the comma.

example.q: Reading the newspaper, the tea got cold. What is wrong?
steps: The tea did not read the newspaper.
The phrase and the subject do not match.
example.answer: The participle dangles; a person must be the subject: Reading the newspaper, I let the tea go cold.

patterns.name: Inversion after negative openers
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence opens with never, hardly, no sooner, rarely, not only, seldom or little.
steps: Spot the negative opener.
Put the helper verb before the subject.
If no helper exists, add do, does or did.
patterns.why: English flips the subject and the helper after such openers.

example.q: Hardly ___ the class begun when the bell rang. (had / has / did / was)
steps: 'Hardly' opens the sentence, so invert.
The past perfect helper 'had' comes before the subject.

patterns.name: Bare infinitive after let, make, see, hear
patterns.howToSpot: The blank follows let, make, see, hear or help, with an object between.
steps: Spot the verb.
In the active, use the bare verb (no to).
In the passive, add to.
patterns.why: These verbs are followed by an object and a bare infinitive.

example.q: The teacher made the boy ___ the answer. (repeat / to repeat / repeating)
steps: 'Made' is followed by a bare infinitive.
Choose 'repeat'.

patterns.name: Stop, remember, forget, try
patterns.howToSpot: The blank follows stop, remember, forget, try or regret and both forms look possible.
steps: Read the meaning.
Verb + to: a purpose or a task ahead.
Verb + -ing: an action already done or an experiment.
patterns.why: The form tells the reader whether the action is past or still to come.

example.q: Please remember ___ the letter on your way. (to post / posting)
steps: It is a task still ahead.
Use 'to post'.

patterns.name: So, neither and nor agreement
patterns.howToSpot: A second clause starts with so, neither or nor and refers to the first clause.
steps: Positive first clause: so + helper + subject.
Negative first clause: neither or nor + helper + subject.
Copy the helper of the first clause.
patterns.why: The reply agrees or disagrees with the first clause and flips the helper.

example.q: She can swim, and so ___ her brother. (can / does / is / will)
steps: The first clause has 'can'.
Copy it: 'so can her brother'.

revision: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, deny, practise + gerund.
want, hope, decide, refuse, manage, promise + to + verb.
